Compost, mulch, humus and organic matter: what actually happens?

Leaves, grass, prunings, roots, compost, mulch, humus... A garden brings together many forms of organic matter. They all belong to the same cycle, but they aren't the same thing. The most important difference may not be what something is called exactly, but what happens to it in the soil.

It starts with plant residue

A plant draws water and nutrients from the soil and uses carbon dioxide from the air to grow. In doing so, it produces organic matter: leaves, stems, roots, fruit. When that plant matter dies, a new phase begins. Leaves fall to the ground, roots die off, a plant gets harvested or decays, prunings end up in the garden. That material becomes food for soil life.

Mulch: material on top of the soil

Lay plant residue on top of the soil, and we call it mulch. So mulch isn't a specific kind of material, but a way of using organic matter: as a layer on the soil. Leaves, straw, wood chips, grass, and even compost can all serve as mulch. A mulch layer does something useful right away — it covers and protects the soil — while at the same time being slowly broken down by fungi, bacteria, small soil creatures and other organisms. The mulch disappears gradually, but the substances it's made of don't all disappear the same way or at the same speed. view all pros and cons

Compost: an intermediate step

You can also put plant residue on the compost heap first. There, soil organisms break it down: part of the easily degradable material disappears as carbon dioxide, water and heat, while other substances are transformed and remain in the compost. Given enough time, this produces a dark, crumbly material in which the original plant residue is largely no longer recognisable. But compost isn't a final destination — once you add it to the soil, the breakdown simply continues.

So what happens in the soil?

This is where it gets interesting. Organic matter consists of all kinds of different substances: some easily broken down, others much harder. Soil life breaks the material down step by step. Among other things, this produces:

  • nutrients that can become available to plants again;
  • carbon dioxide;
  • water;
  • new biomass of bacteria and fungi;
  • and organic substances that can remain in the soil for much longer.

Breakdown happens relatively fast at first, then increasingly slowly. So part of the material can disappear within a short time, while other organic substances can remain present in the soil for decades or even much longer.

So where does humus actually come from?

Humus is often presented as the end product of decomposition: what's left once the easily degradable substances are gone. That picture is useful, but reality is a bit more complicated. Organic matter in the soil consists of different fractions. Part of it is young and easily broken down, another part far more stable. That more stable organic matter can also bond with mineral soil particles and contribute to stable soil aggregates — this is the organic matter we in the garden often refer to as humus.

So humus isn't simply "compost that's become old enough". Part of the compost breaks down quickly, part feeds soil life, part supplies nutrients, and another part remains present much longer as more stable organic matter.

Organic matter is more than humus

When a soil analysis shows, say, 3% organic matter, that doesn't mean the soil consists of 3% humus. Organic matter is the umbrella term for organic material in the soil. This can include, among other things:

  • fresh or partially broken-down plant residue;
  • root remains;
  • remains of soil organisms;
  • easily degradable organic substances;
  • more stable organic matter;
  • organic matter bound to mineral soil particles.

The different fractions behave differently. The easily degradable fractions are mainly important as food and an energy source for soil life, and release nutrients as they break down. The more stable fractions remain present much longer and play an important role in the soil's physical and chemical properties.

Why do we want organic matter in our soil?

Because it does far more than just supply nutrients. Organic matter:

  • feeds soil life;
  • helps hold and make nutrients available;
  • contributes to water-holding capacity;
  • helps mineral soil particles clump into stable aggregates;
  • promotes good soil structure;
  • contributes to good pore structure and aeration.

So it isn't just about "feeding the plant". Part of the organic material mainly matters for soil life, another part for soil structure, and yet another part supplies nutrients directly or indirectly.

The soil isn't a storage cupboard

Organic matter doesn't just sit there. Organic material is constantly being added and broken down: plant residue, roots, mulch, compost, manure and remains of soil organisms keep arriving, while soil life breaks material down into nutrients, CO₂, water and new organic compounds. Part of that organic matter is retained longer and contributes to the soil's stable stock. The eventual organic matter content is therefore the result of the balance between input and breakdown: if breakdown outpaces input, the level drops; if input is enough to compensate for breakdown, the level stays roughly stable.

Not everything you add sticks around equally long

That's an important point if you want to build up organic matter in your soil. Fresh crop residue contains relatively large amounts of easily degradable material. Compost and old manure contain, on average, a larger share of more stable organic matter. Part of what you add is already gone after a year; another part stays present for much longer. That's why people sometimes talk about effective organic matter: the portion of the applied organic matter still present in the soil after one year. But even that effective organic matter isn't permanent — it too keeps breaking down afterwards.

You can also picture that whole movement visually: from plant residue, via mulch or a compost heap, to soil organic matter that soil life further processes into nutrients, more stable organic matter and CO₂ — after which the cycle begins again.

So the goal isn't to preserve organic matter at all costs. A living soil needs to break down organic matter — without breakdown, nutrients aren't released and soil life has no food. What matters is that enough organic material is added to compensate for breakdown, while part of that organic matter can be held in the soil for the longer term.

Plant residue, mulch, compost, living roots and active soil life aren't separate tricks. They're all part of the same cycle — and humus isn't its endpoint, just the part that stays on the road the longest.
